slides: Now let's calculate a circle's area and circumference. These are two very basic formulas, and we use them a lot in exam questions.

slides.say: Here's a circle with radius r. The area of a circle is the space inside it, and its formula is pi r squared. We'll see why in a moment.
at: Here's a circle with radius r

slides.say: The circumference is the length all the way around the circle, and its formula is two pi r.
at: the length all the way around

slides.say: The symbol pi stands for a fixed number. The letter r is our radius. Notice that only the area formula has r squared. Area is measured in square centimeters. Circumference is a length, measured in centimeters.
at: only the area formula has r squared

slides.say: We used pi in the circumference formula earlier. Now let's see what that number means on the picture. Take a circle, and here is its diameter, d.
at: Now let's see what that number means

slides.say: Now peel off the circumference, and lay it out as a straight line.
How many times does the diameter fit into it? Once, twice, three times, and a little bit is left over.
So the circumference is three diameters and a bit. One diameter is two r, so three diameters are six r. So the circumference is a bit more than six r.
at: So the circumference is three diameters

slides.say: And the formula says the circumference is two pi r. So two pi is a bit more than six, and pi is a bit more than three.
at: So two pi is a bit more than six
and pi is a bit more than three

slides.say: Now, why is the area pi r squared? Let's cut the circle into equal slices, like a pizza. Here are eight equal slices.
Now let's lay the slices in a row, one pointing up, the next pointing down. Together they make a shape that is almost a rectangle.
The height of this almost-rectangle is the radius r. Its long edge is made from half of the circle's curved edge. So that length is half the circumference. Half of two pi r is pi r.
The area of a rectangle is its length times its height. So the area is about pi r times r, which is pi r squared.
With eight slices, the edges are still bumpy, so it's not exactly a rectangle. But the thinner the slices, the closer it gets to a real rectangle. That's why the area of the circle is pi r squared.
So pi is a number. It's a fixed number, always the same. It's not an unknown like x or y in an equation.

It just isn't a round number. Pi is three point one four one five nine, and so on. Its digits after the decimal point never end, so instead of writing them, we give it a special sign, the letter pi. That's easier to write and easier to see in the formula.
at: Pi is three point one four one five nine

slides.say: So the area, pi r squared, is a bit more than three times r squared. For a rough comparison, like the next one, that's all we need to know about pi. It's a bit more than three. We need its first digits, three point one four, only when the choices are close ranges of numbers.
at: is a bit more than three times

slides.say: For example, is four pi more than twelve? Four times three is twelve, and pi is a bit more than three, so four pi is a bit more than twelve. Yes.
at: is four pi more than twelve

slides.say: And when the answers have pi in them, keep the pi. Don't replace it with a rounded decimal.
Let's see simple examples. Say the radius is six.
The area is pi r squared, so pi times six squared. Six squared is thirty-six, so the area is thirty-six pi.
at: so the area is thirty-six pi

slides.say: The circumference is two pi r, so two pi times six, which is twelve pi.
I put six in place of the radius and found the area. I put six in place of the radius and found the circumference.
Now a circle with a diameter of fourteen. Careful here. The formulas use the radius, not the diameter.
at: Now a circle with a diameter

slides.say: So first, the radius is half of fourteen, which is seven.
The area is pi times seven squared, which is forty-nine pi, and not pi times fourteen squared. The circumference is two pi times seven, which is fourteen pi.
at: The area is pi times seven squared
The circumference is two pi times seven

slides.say: Another example. I don't know the radius, but I'm given that the circumference is twenty-two pi. Let's find the radius.
I put it into the circumference formula. Two pi r equals twenty-two pi.
We want r alone, so we divide both sides by two pi. On the left I get r. On the right, the pi on top and the pi on the bottom cancel, and twenty-two divided by two is eleven. So the radius is eleven.
I used the formula backwards. Instead of going from the radius to the circumference, I went from the circumference to the radius.
Now a circle whose area is a hundred twenty-one pi. Again, I don't know the radius. I put the area into the formula, so pi r squared equals a hundred twenty-one pi.
Divide both sides by pi, and r squared is a hundred twenty-one. Take the root of both sides, and r is eleven.
Negative eleven, times itself, also gives a hundred twenty-one. But it isn't relevant here. A radius is a length, so it must be positive.

slides: So from the radius we find the area and the circumference, and from the area or the circumference we find the radius.

slides.say: One more idea that the exam likes, wheels. A wheel that rolls without slipping covers exactly one circumference in one full turn. Look at the red point. After one turn, it's at the bottom again, one circumference further.
Say a wheel has a radius of ten centimeters. One turn is two pi times ten, which is twenty pi centimeters.
at: One turn is two pi times ten

slides.say: How many turns does it make along a road of ten pi meters? First the same units. One meter is a hundred centimeters, so ten pi meters are a thousand pi centimeters.

Each turn covers twenty pi, so to count the turns, we divide the road by one turn. The pi's cancel, and a thousand divided by twenty is fifty. So the wheel makes fifty turns. Now let's see an exam question. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next video.
at: and a thousand divided by twenty
